readerTitle: Should a dentist run ads? Three questions before you pay
caseNote: 가상 사례 (치과, 산업용 컨베이어 벨트 제조사, 일정 관리 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 광고를 할지 말지는 '광고가 효과 있나'가 아니라 '광고가 없었으면 오지 않았을 고객 한 명을 얼마에 데려오고, 그 고객이 몇 년 동안 얼마를 남기며, 마지막에 쓴 돈도 그만큼 하는가'로 판단한다.
misconception: 광고 대행사가 보고한 신규 고객 수로 나누면 고객 한 명당 비용이 나온다. 평균 비용이 고객 가치보다 낮으면 예산을 더 늘려도 된다.

sources.text: 마케팅 표준 개념: 고객 획득 비용과 고객 생애 가치 비교, 증분 효과(광고가 없었어도 왔을 고객 제외), 한계 수익 체감

factChecks.note: 치과 계산: 환자 1명이 연 $300 × 평균 4년 = $1,200. 대행사 주장 $2,000 ÷ 20명 = $100. 실제 증분 8명 기준 $2,000 ÷ 8 = $250. 첫 스케일링이 남기는 돈 $60은 가정. 예산 2배: 추가 10명 중 절반(5명)만 증분이면 $2,000 ÷ 5 = $400.
제조사 계산: 전시회 $15,000 ÷ 3곳 = $5,000(주장). 실제 신규 1곳 = $15,000. 거래처 1곳당 연 $5,000을 남기므로 회수 3년, 평균 8년 거래 시 $40,000.

cards.title: Should a dentist run ads?
body: A dentist with a busy two-chair practice gets a call from an ad agency. *"Give us $2,000 a month and we'll bring you 20 new patients."*
That's $100 a patient. It sounds like an easy yes. Three ideas from this unit say it's worth checking first.

image.label: Dentist's desk with an ad agency proposal
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 치과 접수대 위에 "20 new patients / $2,000"라고 적힌 제안서 한 장, 옆에 칫솔 모양 펜. 뒤로 빈 진료 의자 하나와 찬 의자 하나. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: The agency's offer is on your desk.
body: A patient who stays leaves about $300 a year after treatment costs, and stays around four years. That's about $1,200 each.

options.text: Sign up. $100 for a $1,200 patient is a bargain
options.feedback: You get speed, but you trust the agency's count. Some of those 20 may have found you anyway. That's the question of **whether marketing caused the sale**.

options.text: Decline. Good dentists grow by word of mouth
options.feedback: You avoid wasted spend, but you may skip patients worth $1,200 each. Word of mouth and ads can work together.

options.text: Try it for two months and ask every new patient how they found you
options.feedback: You pay a little to learn the real number: how many patients came *because of* the ads. That is the cost that matters.

cards.title: Twenty patients, but not twenty new ones.
body: Twelve of the "ad patients" had a friend's referral or typed the practice's name into a search. They clicked the ad on the way. The real cost per extra patient is **$250**, not $100.

cards.title: Paying for customers: judge the years, not the visit.
body: A first cleaning leaves about $60. Against a $250 ad cost, that visit loses money.

But **paying for customers** means comparing the cost to everything a customer leaves over time. Here that's $250 against about $1,200. The ads pay for themselves in under a year of an average patient's visits.

image.label: Scale: $250 ad cost vs $1,200 patient value
image.brief: 저울 인포그래픽. 한쪽에 "$250 to win a patient" 작은 동전 더미, 다른 쪽에 4년치 달력 위 "$1,200 over 4 years" 큰 더미. 첫 칸 "First visit $60"은 흐리게 표시.

cards.title: The next $2,000 buys less.
body: The agency now suggests doubling to $4,000. It expects 10 more patients. If half would have come anyway, that's 5 truly new at **$400 each**.
That's **diminishing returns**: each extra dollar reaches people farther away or less ready to book. Still under $1,200 on paper, but only worth it if a chair is free to see them.

cards.title: Your best number is also your weakest.
body: The $1,200 is an estimate. Ads with a "first cleaning $49" coupon can pull in price shoppers who leave after one visit. Track how long ad patients actually stay.
Small tests are noisy, too. A slow August or one busy referrer can swing a two-month result. Treat it as a rough guide and check again later.

cards.title: A trade show for conveyor belts.
body: You make replacement conveyor belts for warehouses. A trade show booth cost $15,000 and led to 3 new accounts. Your sales lead says 2 were already talking to you before the show.
Each account leaves about $5,000 a year and stays around 8 years. Was the show worth it?

options.text: Yes. $5,000 per account, paid back in a year
options.feedback: Right conclusion, wrong math. You counted two accounts that **marketing didn't cause**, so the show looks three times cheaper than it was.

options.text: Count only the one new account: $15,000, paid back in 3 years, worth about $40,000
options.feedback: You compare the real cost of one extra customer to what it leaves over its life. That's **paying for customers**, counted honestly.

options.text: No. $15,000 for a single account is too expensive
options.feedback: You protect cash this year but ignore the $40,000 the account leaves over eight years.

cards.title: A scheduling app's ad budget.
body: Your app charges $20 a month. Each user costs $4 a month to serve and stays about 10 months, so a paying customer is worth $160.
You spend $10,000 a month on search ads and get 80 paying customers: $125 each. But the first $7,000 brought 70. The last $3,000 brought only 10. What next?

options.feedback: The average hides the edge. The last $3,000 bought customers at $300 each, so more spend would cost even more. That's **diminishing returns**.

options.text: Trim back toward $7,000 and move the rest to cheaper keywords or retention
options.feedback: You give up some growth but stop paying $300 for $160 customers. Judge each extra dollar, not the average.

options.text: Stop ads. The margin is too thin
options.feedback: Safe, but the first $7,000 bought customers at $100 each. You'd lose the spend that clearly works.

cards.softwareNote: Also ask how many signups came from people who searched your app's name. Those users were likely coming anyway.

cards.title: Before you pay for ads, ask three questions.
list: **Did the ad cause it?** Count only customers who wouldn't have come anyway.
**Is the price right?** Compare that cost to what a customer leaves over years, not one visit.
**Does the last dollar still work?** Averages hide expensive extra spend.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** ask your last ten new customers how they first heard of you. Compare that to what your ad reports claim.
